---
title: "Generational Understanding"
author: "DK"
date: "2026-01-11"
categories: [understanding, hardships]
---

Twice a month, we meet as a group of men ranging from eighteen to over ninety.

The median and mean age of the group skews towards 60s or even 70s.

The dynamics changed recently with a "fresh infusion".

Our Ward boundaries were adjusted, and suddenly, we gained twenty sets of newlywed couples.

We acknowledge one another, renew friendships, plan services and learn anew gospel principles.

Under the direction of the quorum presidency, we adopted a format that isn't practiced at this level of gathering.

Three of the older quorum members are invited and a younger person is designated to ask questions.

On lessons learned in life.

However, today the set up was different.

An older person, a retired university professor asked questions and the panel were 3 young men that recently joined the group.

![](images/IMG_8066.JPG)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

There is a saying, 젊어서 고생은 사서도 한다.

> “Even hardship, when you are young, is something worth buying.”

Hardship builds character.

Suffering is not a debt to be avoided, but an investment to be made.

It seemed, no matter the question, the older generation had a wealth of experiences they can relate to and make connections as to how it helped them navigate in this life.

For those in the older group, life begins to offer an alternate interpretation, often around the time the grandchildren arrive.

At that stage, life feels like a "win-win" scenario:

-   **The Hardships** are a win in the "Experience" column.

-   **The Favorable Outcomes** are an entry in the "Grateful" register.

But what about the younger group?

They are currently in the thick of the "buying" stage.

They are paying for their future character with current stress, young marriages, and the uncertainty of a world that feels increasingly complex.

We had seen and heard the mountaintop perspective.

These three young men were speaking as they were climbing.

![](images/20260110_170638%20(1).jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The moderator, guided the discussion with insight inducing questions.

He asked about the specific distractions of the modern world and the exact moments where spiritual self-sufficiency begins.

Finally, he posed this inquiry:

> "What is one thing that would help the older generation better understand you—the rising generation?"

They described a world that feels like a constant barrage of impending crises.

For them, "hopelessness" isn't a lack of character; it is a rational response to a stream of endless catastrophe.

Comparing with the older generation—who lived through eras of what now seem like heroic deeds—and they wondered:

> Are there any adventures left for us?

The older men in the room have lived their adventures and have paid their dues.

They fulfilled their portion of the social and spiritual contract in a world that felt simpler, more linear.

This younger generation is being offered a "hybrid contract"—one that either doesn't exist in the physical world or doesn't reflect the reality they face every day.

The discussion brought to mind the words of Morrie Schwartz:

> "If the culture doesn't work, don't buy it."

He believed in creating your own authentic culture to find fulfillment, rather than conforming to one that promotes greed or shame.

The older men of the group chose service, family, and faith over the status symbols sold by the world.

They built a culture that works.

Now, I see the young people in our group beginning that same difficult journey.

They are distancing themselves and choosing not to "buy" the hopelessness of the digital age.

Instead of signing onto a broken cultural contract, they are signing with the Source.

> “Ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”
